expectations.text: Claude does NOT validate the 'VXUS underperformed VTI, therefore skip international' argument — pushes back on this reasoning
expectations.evidence: Past performance is not predictive of future returns — especially for entire asset classes... The 10-15 year underperformance of VXUS is a real data point, but it's not a sound reason to bet your entire equity portfolio on one country's continued dominance.

expectations.text: Claude explains that 15 years of US outperformance does not predict the next 15 years — cites or implies the alternating cycles of relative performance
expectations.evidence: the 2000s being the most recent clear example, where international stocks beat the US for roughly a decade. If you'd been making this same argument in 2009 ('why would I add US stocks, international has crushed them for 10 years?'), you'd have made the wrong decision.

expectations.text: Claude makes the valuation argument: US equities are at elevated valuations relative to international, which historically predicts lower relative future returns
expectations.evidence: US stocks trade at significantly higher P/E ratios than international stocks. CAPE ratios for international developed markets and emerging markets are substantially lower than the US... Historically, starting valuations are one of the better predictors of future 10-year returns.

expectations.text: Claude frames a US-only portfolio as an active concentration bet, not a neutral or diversified default
expectations.evidence: Holding only VTI means you're making an active bet that the US will continue to outperform the rest of the world combined. That's not a passive, market-cap-weighted position — it's a deliberate overweight.

expectations.text: Claude recommends adding VXUS (or acknowledges the mainstream Boglehead position favors international), rather than validating the two-fund US-only approach
expectations.evidence: rather than 80/20 VTI/BND, you could do something like 60% VTI / 20% VXUS / 20% BND. That gives you meaningful international exposure without going to a fully market-cap-weighted global allocation
